utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Mr. Tieger, you have a new team member.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, Your Honours. We are joined by Mr. Julian Nicholls to my left today, in addition to myself and Mr. Reid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Welcome, Mr. Nicholls. If the witness could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before we do that, I just want to let you know Peter Robinson is now appearing with Dr. Karadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed you. Welcome, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, could you take a solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a seat. My understanding is that this witness is enjoying the protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion, not the voice distortion. Am I correct, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, so you will be called by your pseudonym during the course of the -- your evidence at the Tribunal, and your face will not be broadcast. I understand that such situations are explained to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I was told that there was a preliminary matter from the accused to raise, but I'm not sure whether we need to hear that in the presence of the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, good afternoon. I said last time that I would like to clarify a matter, and you said that we'll leave it for next time. Of course, this can be done during the break before the witness comes into the courtroom next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before the witness goes ahead and before I start my cross-examination, in actual fact, I'd also like to ask something, raise an issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Nicholls, could you start, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. As I told you before, it's going to be a little bit different this time than when you testified before. We're going to put in your testimony that you've given earlier, and I have to ask a few questions about that before we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But first could I have the pseudonym sheet. It should not be broadcast. This is 65 ter number 90178.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, if you can just look at the name on that piece of paper on the screen in front of you, read it to yourself quietly, and just could you confirm that your name is written there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm done with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If that could be admitted under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be Exhibit P767, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let me just ask you these questions about your earlier testimony so we can put those statements in. Can you please confirm to the Trial Chamber that you listened to the audio recordings of your entire testimony in the Popovic case, and you also listened to the -- your testimony in the Slobodan Milosevic case, including the entire cross-examination by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also confirm for the Trial Chamber that if you were asked the same questions today -- sorry. Let me go back. And can you confirm that when you listened to those audio recordings they were an accurate record of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you were asked the same questions today as in those prior testimony, would your answers be the same? Could you confirm that? With the exception of some additional clarifying information about one of your brothers that we'll -- we'll get to soon?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, now I'd like to admit - I think this is the way we're doing it - the statement which is 65 ter 90112, which would be under seal because that contains the complete testimony including private session, and we have a public version which is 90112A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You meant to tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one clarifying question. When there are several transcripts, the Chamber order was for you to produce just one transcript. Otherwise, an amalgamated statement. So technically, this practice is in breach of that order, and then that's the first question. And the second question is why only the part of that cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll explain that, Your Honour. I did not intend to breach the order. The -- this is essentially an amalgamated statement. The purpose of including simply part of the cross-examination from the Milosevic case was because that was an area that the witness was cross-examined on more extensively and more -- and more -- in a more lengthy and perhaps comprehensive manner than was in the Popovic cross-examination. So there is very little overlapping evidence in those two transcripts. Mr. Milosevic, in his cross-examination, concentrated primarily on a different area, and that's why I've included just his cross-examination and not the cross-examination by others in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence believes that this is a very important part, and as you'll see in due course, the Defence will be focusing precisely on that part, although this is all cumulative. But in any case, I have to devote most of my time to that particular portion, and later on I'll be sending the Trial Chamber a kind request asking them for certain changes with respect to the other part that this witness is going to deal with, because the cross-examination will focus mostly on that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That is why -- I thought that might be the case, that Mr. Karadzic would think that area was important, and that's why it was included as well as the Popovic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those will be admitted as one amalgamated statement. Mr. Doraiswamy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 90112 will be Exhibit P768, under seal, and 90112A will be Exhibit P769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll now read a short summary of the witness's evidence. The witness was born in Zvornik municipality and grew up there. At the beginning of March 1993, he and his family were forced from Kamenica by Bosnian Serb forces. At this time, his wife and children fled to Tuzla, and he fled to Konjevic Polje. He stayed in Konjevic Polje for six days. Serb forces in Tumace then opened fire on Konjevic Polje and the witness fled to Pervane. He stayed in Pervane for two days before leaving for Srebrenica with his two brothers, and they remained in Srebrenica until the fall of the enclave on 11 July 1995. The days before 11 July were rife with panic, in the witness's words, for the population of the Srebrenica enclave. On 11 July, in the face of the Bosnian Serb advance on the enclave, the entire population of Srebrenica fled. Some went to Potocari, others to the woods. The witness and one of his brothers assembled with thousands of other Muslim men in the nearby village of Susnjari to begin the trek towards Tuzla. Another brother who had a disability, was an invalid, chose to go to Potocari. This brother managed to cross to Muslim-held territory. The witness spent the night of 11 July in Susnjari along with approximately 15.000 to 20.000 other Muslim men, according to his estimate. On 12 July, the group of Muslim men set off from Susnjari in a long column heading towards Tuzla. There were 400 to 500 armed men, armed Muslim men in the column, mostly toward the front of the column, and later that afternoon the witness was in the last group of the column to leave with his brother. He and his brother were not armed. He spent the night of 12 to 13 July in the woods with others from the column. On 13 July, the next day, Bosnian Serb soldiers with megaphones called on the people in the column in the woods to surrender. Around this time the witness saw two Muslim men commit suicide, one with a grenade. The other shot himself in the head. That afternoon at around 1500 hours, he and many others decided to surrender to Serb soldiers who were calling them. These prisoners, approximately a thousand of them, over a thousand of them, according to the witness's estimate, were lined up in rows in a large group in a meadow in Sandici next to the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. There were also some women, girls, and boys present amongst the prisoners at Sandici meadow. About a dozen boys under 15 and some women and girls were permitted to get onto buses carrying Muslim women and children from Srebrenica which were passing by on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road taking these people from Potocari. That afternoon, General Mladic came to Sandici meadow and he addressed the prisoners, promising them that they would be exchanged. And the prisoners applauded General Mladic when he said that. Later that evening, a large number of trucks and buses arrived at Sandici. The prisoners boarded those buses and trucks and were taken away to Bratunac. He spent the night, the witness spent the night, 13 to 14 July, in Bratunac inside the truck he'd been placed on, parked outside buildings of Vihor garages. During the night some prisoners were taken off of these parked trucks. Soldiers would shout out for prisoners from certain villages, and those who answered were taken off the trucks. The witness could hear sounds of beating, screams, shots being fired, and these prisoners were not seen again and were not returned to the trucks. The witness himself did not see any prisoners being shot from inside of his truck, but this is what he heard around him. The next day, 14 July, the trucks and buses left Bratunac in a long convoy, 20 to 30 vehicles the witness saw, and headed north towards Zvornik via Konjevic Polje. In Divic, a village just south of Zvornik, the witness saw a white UN APC. The convoy of vehicles continued to Karakaj, north of Zvornik, and then turned left in the general direction of Tuzla. The witness hoped, and the others, that they were being taken to Tuzla for an exchange. However, instead this convoy of trucks and buses went to Orahovac and stopped at the elementary school there. The UN APC was parked there in the schoolyard, and the witness realised it had actually been captured by Bosnian Serb soldiers. The witness and hundreds and hundreds of other Muslim men, along with four young children aged approximately 10 to 14, placed in the gym of the elementary school at Orahovac and kept there as the gym kept filling up with prisoners. He and the other prisoners were forced to leave some of their clothing in a large pile on the way to the gym. The witness was told to take off his jacket and leave it there. Other men were told to take off their shirts --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Objection, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I would object, really. Of course, if -- if -- [Interpretation] In any case, if you want to hear this for dramatic reasons, the details of this to be presented, that's fine, but it will take away a lot of my time, and this is also a form of cumulative testimony in view of the fact that in the previous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. This is unacceptable. This is a summary of the witness's evidence on the part of the Prosecution for the benefit of you and the public, and the Chamber as well. This is not part of evidence. You will be given ample opportunity to cross-examine this witness, so I would like you not to interrupt this, giving the summary of the evidence by the Prosecution. You can cross-examine the witness later on. Mr. Nicholls, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The gym was packed and the witness and the other prisoners had to sit closely packed together as it became full. It was very hot that -- on 14 July, and the prisoners were given some water but not nearly enough water for everybody, and they were very thirsty. From the time of his detention in Sandici meadow and up until his eventual escape, the witness was given some water on different occasions but no food. And the witness observed that none of the other prisoners were given food and none of the ill or wounded were given medical care. Also, the witness observed that at no time were the prisoners registered, listed, or counted by their captors. They remained in the Orahovac school for a few hours and sometimes the guards would fire shots into the walls and ceiling to keep the prisoners quiet. Some officers arrived at the school and the prisoners were ordered to stand up in rows and face one end of the gym, and it was about this time that one of the prisoners objected and said that these men should not be killed. Guards took this prisoner outside and a shot was fired that the witness heard, and the man did not come back. Then another prisoner was taken out and again a shot was heard. Again, the prisoner did not come back. Once the officers left, the soldiers began taking prisoners in groups through a small room next to the gym where they were given a cup of water by a female soldier, blindfolded, taken outside and placed in TAM trucks. And the witness estimates that approximately 30 prisoners could fit in the back of one of these TAM trucks. Prisoners were told that they were being taken to a camp in Bijeljina as they got on the trucks. However, the trucks drove just a very short distance to a field in Orahovac and the prisoners were told then to get off the trucks. The men were lined up in rows and shot. The witness managed to survive by feigning death as he lay under the body of another victim. And the witness observed that approximately every 10 to 15 minutes a new truck full of prisoners would arrive, and those prisoners would be killed in the same manner. These killings continued for hours. After nightfall, a loader truck arrived with its lights on, and as it continued, the witness lay still and heard some of the executioners speaking and calling to one another, and they called their leader by name. The witness recognised the first name and the distinctive voice of this leader of the executioners as a long-time co-worker who he knew was from the village of Orahovac. The leader told the other soldiers to collect ammunition and go to a nearby field to continue killing people. The soldiers then left and continued killing prisoners at a nearby field. Later that night while the soldiers were distracted, the witness was able to escape into the woods. As he ran away, he got turned around at one point and found himself back at the killing site, and he saw that most of the field was covered in bodies. He also noticed that not all of the prisoners were dead. He could hear sounds coming from a wounded man. After several very difficult days of -- as he describes it, of moving and hiding, he managed to reach safety in Muslim-held territory. That's the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I have just very few questions for you, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session just for a short background question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to ask you now just a -- a few questions about the events of 11 July 1995, and about what happened to you and your two brothers at that time. Now, first of all, you've testified that it was on 11 July that you and your brothers, and in fact the entire population, left Srebrenica. Could you tell the Chamber why was it that you decided to leave Srebrenica that day? Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, we had to leave because the Serb forces threatened us, especially Radovan Karadzic. One year previously he said he would take his revenge on the citizens of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, what were you concerned about would happen if you'd stayed, if you hadn't left 11 July? Why exactly did you leave?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, we left because we were frightened, and the thing that we were frightened of happened to us en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, without saying his name, one of your brothers, you testified, went to Potocari and managed to leave safely. Can you just tell us very briefly how he managed to accomplish that, what he told you about how he was able to leave Potocari?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, when he reached Potocari, they had already begun separating people, and a Serb soldier told him to jump up on the truck, and he had -- he couldn't do that because he had crutches. And then another one told him to get into another bus, and he got into that and that's how he managed to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, if I may go into private session just for a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I think if I understood your ruling before correctly, now is when I would tender the exhibits I have not shown the witness but that formed part of his testimony in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that those lists were provided to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objections, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Robinson? Who is going to deal with the objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In your order you indicated that I would only intervene at the request of Mr. Karadzic. So he will be dealing with all of them unless he requests otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have any objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The Chamber also had the opportunity to go through the list, and then all of them are relevant and of probative value, and we find that all of them form indispensable and inseparable part of the evidence. As such we admit them all. Could we give the -- there are five items. We can give the exhibit number right now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 02869 will be Exhibit P770; 65 ter number 21964 will be Exhibit P771; 65 ter number 2870 will be Exhibit P772; 65 ter number 02872 will be Exhibit P773; and 65 ter number 02875 will be Exhibit P774.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one more, which is not as important. It's 65 ter number 21965. That was simply the pseudonym sheet in the prior testimony. It forms part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But hasn't been assigned a separate number yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P775, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to cross-examine this witness, but please bear in mind that this witness's identity is protected. Whenever there's a danger of revealing the identity of the witness, you should ask to go into private session. Do you understand? With that caveat, let's start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I would just like to say one thing before I start with my cross-examination and also draw your attention to what Madam Uertz-Retzlaff said at a Status Conference of the 17th of August, 2009. This is on page 156, where she said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, instead of giving submissions, I would like you to start your questioning. Just put your questions to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I wanted to say was that the Srebrenica part as it relates to 95 was something that we're a little surprised by. We thought we would be dealing with that later, but that's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have provided five statements so far?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You participated in two reports, and you testified four times.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Five times.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we say -- of course this was strenuous, but could we say that you were a successful witness and that perhaps you're even proud of your achievement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes, I am a successful witness, but let me tell you the truth. It's not my desire to be a successful witness and to speak lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you live now where you used to live before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You live in the federation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't live in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to know, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, twofold. One, going into an inquiry in public session of where a protected witness lives is heading for trouble; and two, it's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one cautionary note. I can see it coming, and that is the pace of the question and answer and the need for a pause between question and answer when the witnesses are speaking the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your warning. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would rather say that I asked him where he did not live instead of where he does live, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm interested in is this: Why did you seek protective measures if you are a successful witness -- I don't want to say that you're a favourite witness of the Prosecution, because they don't like that, but why did you do such a big job?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, you know why. Because there are people who share your beliefs, who would like to get rid of me. So I don't want everybody to know where I live for that reason. I'm speaking, and I do not wish to say one more word more than is absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know any witnesses who my supporters executed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I don't know, but I'm afraid for myself. I'm not really interested too much about others. I'm only speaking about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this whole line of why the witness has sought protective measures. He's had them granted in several -- in all the prior case because the Trial Chambers in those cases have found that they were justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I let it go because to a certain extent you may ask some questions, but let's move on your topic. But before we go -- go any further, sir, could you bear in mind the interpreters who are interpreting your questions and answers. So could you wait a little bit, put a pause after the question and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on to your topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You lived and worked in Belgrade more than 18 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How often did you go back to your birthplace?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I would go back every week or every other week depending on when I had my Saturdays free. That's when I would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you would spend a weekend there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see your compatriots in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: What do you mean "compatriots"? Who are my compatriots, Serbs or Croats? We were all compatriots, Bosniaks, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Bosniaks with the same surname as yours.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, there are people with my surname all over Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we are going to show this later on the screen, exactly what I'm thinking of, but tell me, did you follow the events in Bosnia from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I came only when the war was beginning in Bijeljina. The war hadn't started in other places yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You came on the 3rd of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you come?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, it was the Bajram holiday then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. And did you know about the political events and the tensions and the course of events in Bosnia? Were you following that from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, no, we didn't really know all that much in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You didn't come to defend your village, did you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: It was Bajram. And to tell you the truth, it was -- I do have the right to defend my village. Every citizen has the right to defend his village and his country, Mr. Karadzic. A Serb, a Croat, a Gypsy, they're all duty-bound to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina and not to ethnically cleanse it of one people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And who would you defend Kamenica from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: From whoever attacked it, whether it was a Muslim, Croat, a Serb. You defend your country from any enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, I understand how you feel, but could you calm down a bit, and if you need some time, you can take a rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem about a rest. It's a matter of the question. One would defend one's country from any attack, regardless of ethnicity. Fikret Abdic was a Bosniak and our people had to defend themselves from them because he was killing his own people. Whoever attacks the country should be somebody to defend oneself from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Please understand the Defence is entitled to ask you questions. So try to answer as far as you can. Just -- if you don't know, you can say you don't know, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that that is the answer. You defend your country from the enemy, whether it's an enemy from within or from outside. That is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And one further request is for the benefit of the Chamber and the interpreters, just wait a little bit after the question before you start your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, do you know that according to the Cutileiro Plan, your area was supposed to be part of the Muslim entity? It was supposed to be a Muslim canton?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I don't know that. If anybody among the politicians knew that, that's all right, but don't ask me that. I'm not a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you believe that your politicians knew that, because they accepted that agreement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think that they did, but I don't know. I really couldn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Cutileiro's map now. If it's not in e-court, perhaps we can look at it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you are going to show on the map the region where the witness is from, we need to go into private session, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I think that Cutileiro's map is something that we're all familiar with. It's a generally known matter. This is 1D883. 00883; is that right? It doesn't have to be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness what the map looks like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Please don't show it to me. You don't have to show it to me. I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have the map before us on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't accept that at all. If this is something that you divided together with Cutileiro, we did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us where your hometown is here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, my hometown is the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't need you to draw any maps. There are these things that Cutileiro sketched out and you are sticking to that without yielding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're not the only people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is Rastosnica yours?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, Rastosnica is everybody's. If it's a Muslim village, it's a Muslim village; if it's a Serb village, it's a Serb village. Nobody took any villages from anybody. You wanted to drive us out of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to create an ethnically pure territory. You didn't want to have us in Bosnia and Herzegovina any longer. Well, you don't need to go on about that now. Just let me be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please calm down. Just answer the question. Mr. Karadzic, what the witness is saying is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the 3rd of April, 1992. I know the situation. They wanted to drive us out, even had -- if we had given them the whole of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they wanted it to be empty of all Muslims and Croats. They only wanted the Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We're going to prove the opposite, but what I'm asking you now is to show us where your hometown is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know where my hometown is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remove this from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like you and ask again to just answer the question. That's the best way for you to assist the Chamber. Mr. Karadzic, I don't see any point going over --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to look at any maps. Please understand me. Karadzic can look at maps. I don't need to look at maps. I don't need a map. We have a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina in its internationally recognised borders. We're not interested in Republika Srpska or Herceg Bosna. All we're interested is Bosnia. Bosnia is not Croat or Serb or Muslim only. It belongs to all of its citizens, but Karadzic would like to have Bosnia belong to only one people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, as I told you, the Defence, the accused, is entitled to put questions to you. So if you do not know, you can say simply you don't know, but please hear me out. I was about to say something to make it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked that he doesn't show me the map. I don't recognise the map at all. I'm not interested in the map at all. If you're interested in the map, Mr. President, sir, please go ahead. I will not disrupt that. If I had some sort of scarf or something, I would cover the screen so I don't have to look at this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't see any point going over the question of map when the witness has already said he didn't know anything about Cutileiro's map. You can tender this evidence on a separate occasion or through a separate proceedings. I would like you to move on to the next topic, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, I will move on. The point is, though, that his place of birth, we accepted that it would not be in the Serbian canton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have -- you'll have opportunity to make your submission. Please concentrate on putting questions to the witness instead of making submissions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to have document 65 ter 19139 on the screen. This is a Prosecution document. It doesn't have to be broadcast to the public. It can just be restricted to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this a map of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I'm not interested. Well, let me just see. My municipality of Zvornik, I am a protected witness, but my municipality is the municipality of Zvornik. I was born there. I grew up there. I lived there until I was 50 or 60 years old. It cannot be yours. It can only be my municipality. I'm sorry, I don't see which municipality this is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's written there for you at the top.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If it is. I mean, it is the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate on the south the area which we're interested in?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I'm not interested. You were interested in everything, for God's sake, not one thing. You were interested in everything. What are you saying? You were interested in everything. You just wanted no Bosniaks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you testified five times, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I'm sorry to interrupt you for a moment. The question that you must address your mind to, Mr. Witness, is this, that we are the ones, the Judges, who need this information. Whether you are interested or not interested is a matter for you, but you've got to understand that we are interested. We need to know these things in order to make a proper determination of the case. So I understand that this is a difficult exercise for you, but please bear in mind that this is information which we need to conduct this case fairly and properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the entire municipality of Zvornik was ethnically cleansed. It was ethnically cleansed. I don't think that one single Bosniak remained to live in the entire municipality of Zvornik. It's not that he was interested in one or the other part of the municipality. He was interested in the whole of the municipality, one large area, Djulici, Potocari. I have a married sister there. Over 700 people there submitted or handed over their weapons saying, "We don't want war." They were handing over keys of their car saying, "We don't want war." The Serbian Army assembled everyone, women and children, in buses and trucks and sent them off to Tuzla. Over 700 people were executed. It was not -- nothing else was in his interest other than ethnic cleansing and war. He was not interested in just one part of the Zvornik municipality or another part. He was interested in the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you're a very important witness, and your testimony has been incorporated into several judgments finding the accused guilty, so I would like to hear your testimony, and the Prosecution can help you out, but I would like the Registrar -- to ask the Registrar also to help the witness use the electronic pen that he uses for the screen so that he can draw on the map.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this map. What do you want me to tell you about this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, it's not my map. It's a Prosecution map, and it's a geographical map, a normal one without any ethnic division.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: What do you want me to mark in here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I think it might help if we knew exactly what -- what the question was, because I may have missed it, but there hasn't been a clear question about this map and what is asked. The only question was, "Can you indicate the southern area we're interested in," or something, but I think maybe if there's a very clear question, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you answer the question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't, Your Excellency, disclose my intentions to the Prosecution in advance. I have to take the witness statements one by one. Now, he lived in this area, he worked there, and important events took place there until March 1993, and more important and more intensive than the other part of his testimony. So this is where major events took place, and because of that, Mr. Nicholson [sic] sought to introduce it into the Milosevic trial. Now, I want us to establish where these places were, who lived in them and what happened in them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs lived on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or, rather, Zvornik municipality, in their villages. The Bosniaks lived in their own villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's not my question, nor is that the answer that you should be giving. I would like us to focus on your testimony and the places you mentioned in that testimony.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, I don't want to have anything to do with the map. I don't want to mark anything on the map. You can ask me what happened where, but -- and I'll tell you, but I don't want to have anything to do with the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Prosecution instruct their witness as to his duties and assist him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need any assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, sir. Sir, as Judge Morrison advised you, your answering the question is the best way to assist the Chamber to reach -- to find the facts before -- in this case, so I don't find your non-cooperation very helpful. So as far as you can, please try to answer the question. Do you recognise where it is, that which appears before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I don't know this map, and I would have to guess. I don't want to do guesswork. I know the territory, but I'm not interested in the map at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it that your answer is that you do not -- you cannot recognise what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anything he asks me I'll tell him, but I have nothing to do with maps. Nobody every showed me a map before. I don't know what he wants to achieve with this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can move on to -- to a different topic apart from the map. Please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, they're still living there. How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you arrived on the 3rd of April, 1992. Do you know what happened, before you left, to the Serbs living in your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Gone where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, before you left your village.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, they expelled us from their village first. Do you know about that? And do you know about these 122 Serbs, they set fire to six Muslims in a forge. Do you know about that? And they were neighbours. They weren't people who came in from elsewhere. They were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, would you please focus on what I'm asking you and the subject of your testimony. Do you know what happened to those Serbs before the Serbs arrived in your village in March 1993, before that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, what Serbs? There are quite a lot of Serbs there. What Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all the Serbs in your village, to all the Serbs in your village?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I don't know. The minority left, and the majority, well, nobody touched them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. Your Honours, just out of an abundance of caution, I think we might need a redaction on page 29, lines 14 to 18, because of the precise description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Please put your question again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, how many Serbs were there in your two villages when the Serb army entered those villages?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: When the Serb army entered those villages, there were very few Serbs there, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: How should I know? Zvornik? I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the village where there were more Serbs, 301?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say they were all there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You mentioned two brothers, and you had a third brother as well, but you didn't mention him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Don't tell us his name, but could you tell us what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was he killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: In Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the place name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did he die?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: He was killed by a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you repeat the place where your brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what, as I'm a protected witness, I -- it slipped out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you can tell us about your village. This isn't being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me check what I said. Mr. Nicholls, do we need to go into private session in order to hear where his brother was killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour. Just for the name of the -- maybe it would be best if -- I'm not sure, so maybe it would be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, when did that happen and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell me where there was fighting, and was he a sehid or, rather, a fighter?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that first brother of yours, does he have any children?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Boys?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of his sons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, I can't. He just has one son, just one child, a son.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, might we go into private session just for a second to hear the name of the man's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in your statements that your family left before you to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: My family did leave and go to Tuzla, because -- was it on the 30th or 31st of January, 1993? Not a long time before me, just a fortnight before or thereabouts, because we had to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where were the Serbs then in relation to your village, the Serb army, I mean.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: At the time, the Serbs called upon the people to move out of our village, and people escorted women and children, elderly persons so that more people left, and we had to withdraw and move towards Konjevic Polje and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I say, Mr. Witness, that this was a planned, organised evacuation of civilians from your region and from your villages which was carried out by your army, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I put that to you. What you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, certainly not. In 1992, the Serb army moved upon us, set fire to our houses, destroyed our mosques. There were four mosques in the village. And we all moved out. Our families were with us, and we went to the neighbouring municipality. Just a small hamlet was left with just six or seven houses, and the people remained in those households, but the women and children had to be evacuated. Now, after that, we had to organise ourselves to send -- to expel the Serbs from our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But would you please stick to answering my questions, please. You didn't leave with them, and you didn't go to Tuzla. Why?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, here's why: I always thought -- I was wondering what happened to the people when the women and children were arrested. A lot of young girls and women were raped, so heaven forbid that my children should suffer the same fate, and I have two daughters and a son, and I always wondered what would happen if my daughter was killed. I would bury her and move on. God forbid that my child should be raped. And that did happen. Women and mothers and girls were raped -- or, rather, girls were raped before their mother's eyes. And that's why I didn't dare leave. I wanted them to go, and I would await my fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it perhaps because you were necessary as a soldier, and then the army evacuated over 7.000 civilians in order to be better able to fight and you stayed on to fight? Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No. We had men, but we didn't have any weapons. All we had were our bare chests so that others could attack us with howitzers, mortars, and so on. Had we had weapons, we wouldn't have suffered the fate that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you were a soldier of the BH Army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any cold weapons?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: What do you mean? You mean a stick, a pole? Huh. A rifle? You know what you mean by cold weapons? Well, your rifle was a cold weapon if you didn't have any ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, we will put to you documents from your command. You previously omitted to say that you were a soldier of the BH Army. Today you have confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I never denied that. I always said that I was a soldier. I was a JNA soldier, and I was also the other soldier. Well, not a -- not a soldier, really, because we didn't have any weapons. I had to just replace a colleague and do his shift, take up a colleague's shift, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statements it says that you were not a soldier. Then it says that you were a soldier, then again that you weren't a soldier, and we can see that from your various statements, and we see that you said that you were a member of the Territorial Defence, although the Territorial Defence, in mid-April 1992, also became a part of the BH Army. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: While I was in my village, I was a member of the TO, the Territorial Defence. Afterwards, when I went to Srebrenica, I was no longer a -- I was not a soldier. That's what I meant when I said I wasn't a soldier. Now, when I returned to free territory again, everybody tried to persuade me not to be a soldier, but I wanted to. But while that discussion was going on, the war ended, so I didn't have the right to become a soldier after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you deny that your army had organised the evacuation of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean you don't deny it or you do?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, what you say is not true. The people were lacking food. They couldn't stay there. You know when your house is burnt, well, we didn't even have one nail to take out of the ashes and use it. In 1992, at the beginning of April, you cut our electricity supply off. We had no communication with the town so we had to leave. The food had been burnt in the houses that were set fire to, so the people had to leave in order to find food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just remind you, Witness. Did you receive your electricity from the Visegrad electric power plant?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No. I don't know where we got our electricity from, but I think we got it from Zalukovik, which belonged to Vlasenica or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, sir, that whole area received electricity from Visegrad through the distribution centre that went through Srebrenica, and I assert that the transmission system was disabled by Oric's army in Srebrenica until the end of the war and that is why you didn't have electricity.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, no. At the beginning of the war you personally ordered, I don't know if it was you or the people in Zvornik or wherever, ordered that our electricity be switched off. Even without any war yet starting in our area we were left without electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how exactly did I order that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, of course, you were the number one person. You always go to the head and ask. You never ask the feet for permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, if you say that I was the one who ordered that, I have to get you to be more specific about that. How and when did I make that order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your next -- let's move on to your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this other brother of yours, was he also a soldier?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a cook?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who did he cook for?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: He cooked for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he cook for the army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No. They had an observation post in Slatina. UNPROFOR was there as well. They were just observing there a little bit the movement of the Serbs. The line was quite close, so he was cooking for those who were at the observation post. I mean, he cooked the whole time. He was a baker by trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many fighters from your village joined the unit in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: I don't know how many joined. When we came to Srebrenica, that was when the demilitarisation agreement was signed, so there was nothing to join, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to say that 500 fighters joined from your village alone and significantly strengthen Naser Oric's forces in Srebrenica, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, definitely not. There weren't that many. There weren't that many citizens from our municipality altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your municipality.

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Yes, from my municipality. I'm not talking about Srebrenica. Srebrenica is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, how many people, soldiers and civilians, came to Srebrenica from your municipality in 1993?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know how many of them came. Many of them did come, but when the convoys took the women and children out, most of the women and children left. All those who were left were the elderly and able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to deal a little bit with what was happening in your municipality -- or, rather, first of all, in your village. Can we please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When we are moving to a separate topic, I'm minded to take a break now. So while the -- the witness can be excused from the room. Would the curtain be drawn. I would allow the accused to raise what he meant to raise with the Chamber. Sir, we are going to have a break for 25 minutes. We will be -- we will have a break for 25 minutes. We will adjourn -- we will resume at 4.00. So you may be free to go, to take a rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I would like to draw your attention to what was said at the conference of the 17th of September -- August, 2009. On page 156, when Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said, I'm reading from the middle: "[In English] And I also can say that the Srebrenica part of the case will definitely not -- will definitely be at the end of the Prosecution case, so there is no need to have it all ready by the beginning of trial." [Interpretation] That is why I would kindly ask about the second part of the testimony of this witness that relates to 1995. We summoned the witness again when Srebrenica will be the topic. I will be ready to deal with 1993, and we can complete that today, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may have a say to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to question whether there's any genuine confusion here. I think it was apparent to everyone that that was a reference to the general procedures, the general approach to the case. The fact that issues -- I don't remember the precise context, but if I -- my recollection is that that had to do with whether or not one particular issue had to be disposed of by a particular time. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff was indicating that the bulk of the Srebrenica presentation would be toward the latter part of the case and that could be raised then. It was anything but a reference to the evidence of this particular witness, which has been noticed for a long time, and it's been very clear what this witness's testimony would be. That reference at the Status Conference in no way precludes the full presentation of this witness's evidence or in any way prejudices the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber be advised as to the date when it was noted to the accused that this witness is coming as the third witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was around the 9th of October, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Last year. Thank you very much. We will rise. We will have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we leave, while the witness is still out, I just wanted to mention two or three other things that you promised that I would be given the opportunity to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding cross-examination and examination-in-chief that relates to 1995, this is already done through testimony, statements, adjudicated facts, and so on, but we need to be familiar with the entire Srebrenica case that relates to 1995. Since we were not granted the time we asked for to prepare, and since we relied by what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said, and in view of our priorities and resources, we left the section relating to Srebrenica '95 for later. This is what I wanted to state briefly. The demands of the courtroom are quite substantial, the pace and some other factors, too, so I'm afraid the other services are not actually able to follow all of that. For now I would just like to refer to the matter of translation. I must say that I have engaged my entire family all the way to Canada to translate for me, because I don't expect the documents to be translated on time. I don't have such large resources. My family's translating for me for free. I don't have enough funds to pay for this service. The Tribunal services should be able to keep up with this pace. And I'm doing all I can in order to make the administration of international justice possible, and I'm not trying to obstruct this administration in any way. Should I put down in writing what I asked for last time, and that is to ask for one more person to assist, because Mr. Tieger has as many as he wants, and they change. So also do I need to write my request to receive statements in Serbian? I don't receive transcripts. My associates out in the field or many of them don't speak English, so this would be of help to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come to that after the break. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During the break the Chamber was able to locate the submission Madam Uertz-Retzlaff made during that Status Conference, which reads like this: "Perhaps one point we would appreciate a decision on the 92 bis motion for the expert would be postponed to a later date until everything is ready, and I also can say that Srebrenica part of the case will definitely not -- will definitely be at the end of the Prosecution case, so there's no need to have it all ready by the beginning of the trial." That's what she said. Given this statement, I tend to agree that the accused and the Chamber was always led to believe by the Prosecution that it would bring the Sarajevo component of its case first, then the component dealing with the municipalities, and the Srebrenica component last. Mr. Karadzic was told in the context of denying his request -- request for more preparation time that he didn't need to prepare everything before the trial started, and on my part, I think it's fair that he would have been focusing his preparation on preparing to cross-examine the Sarajevo witnesses. So even if he has known that this witness, KDZ064, would come and talk about Srebrenica since October, he would still be justified in saying that he was devoting his resources preparing for Sarajevo evidence first. That said -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I presume the Court will give me an opportunity to amplify if -- before it renders any decision, but I know I interrupted the Court. I misunderstood the pause to be a completion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I will continue. Thank you. So that said, while it is very -- the Chamber is disappointed by the practice of the Prosecution for not sticking to the -- its earlier representation that Sarajevo would come first and then -- but having said that, given that witness scheduling is a -- is not a matter of exact science and there always has to be some flexibility, so the Chamber is of the view that Mr. Karadzic should continue to cross-examine this witness, and later on, should he find material during his further preparation to address the Srebrenica component of the Prosecution case, then he can always submit a reasoned application to recall this witness for further cross-examination should he consider it to be necessary. So with that, I would like you to continue your cross-examination, including the '95 Srebrenica component of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you have anything to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. I wanted to raise another issue, but if I may respond to the comments of the Court. I want to stress that there was anything but an intentional effort either to mislead the Court or the Defence, and I maintain that the Prosecution has not departed from what it communicated to the Court, and that is that the Srebrenica component would come at the latter part of the case. The question that arose in the context of the 65 ter was whether it was necessary to deal with a particular specific issue related to the Srebrenica component. At that time, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff indicated that that issue would not be overcome by events because the component part of the case, the bulk of the presentation of the evidence related to Srebrenica, was going to -- was not going to come at the beginning of the case. So that specific issue did not need to be resolved. I believe that everyone present at the 65 ter conference at that point understood that, and I think our noticing of the witnesses along with the information presented in connection with what the witness would be testifying to provided ample notice, as I indicated before. And I appreciate the Court's ruling in light of that, but I need to stress this is not a situation where we simply indicate we'll have a witness and that's all the information provided. Virtually everything to which the witness was expected to testify was provided well, well in advance. The second thing is I wanted to dispatch one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm not sure whether I understood you in full. What did you mean by "the context," "in the context of the Rule 65 ter"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was a very limited issue raised: Was it necessary to deal with this expert issue now, or -- because the -- that component part of the case would be over by the time it got dealt with. It needed to be dealt with by the beginning of the case when -- well, by the beginning of the case was the issue then. And because it relates to the overall presentation of the evidence, because the Defence presumably wants to deal with that issue before the component part of the case is completed, that issue was raised. It has very little, if anything, to do with this particular witness who is a percipient witness to the events he experienced and observed. So what was communicated about the order of presentation of the case was related to the issue raised at the 65 ter conference at that moment, and that is, was there any problem with the timing of dealing with this expert issue given the -- the general order in which the case would be presented, and I think it's fair to say that there was not and is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So what I'm suggesting is there was never a preparation that no evidence whatsoever with relation to Srebrenica would be presented prior to a date -- a particular date. It was that the case would be presented in broad components, and that was the general order in which it would be presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let me be clear. Has your plan to present the Srebrenica component of evidence at the later stage been changed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And still -- but still you are minded to introduce some of the components of the Srebrenica case in the early stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As we indicated in the pre-trial brief and in the opening statement, there's clearly a relationship between all components of the case. Therefore, we are providing the Court at the outset of the case with evidence concerning all the components, as the Court can see, so that at least the Court will be -- will have a sufficient initial understanding of the inter-relationship between those component parts of the case. But our intention to focus on -- in general on the component parts of the case in a particular order has not changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So for the benefit of the -- it will be for the benefit of the Chamber as well if you stick to your original plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour, and I think the Court can see how -- the extent to which the Prosecution has attempted to adhere to the witness schedule that was provided last year as the case was continued for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that said, that heard, I would encourage you again to stick to your statements. And then there's another matter you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. The accused raised again the issue of statements, and I think that was raised last week for the first time when the accused said, as far as he remembered, the decision regarding translations did not apply to what he called basic statements. And he said, "And if my understanding is correct," he'd ask that statements in contrast to transcripts be translated. I just -- I want to alert the Court that the accused's understanding is not correct, and the decision of March 26th of last year on that issue explicitly embraced both statements and transcripts. So that should dispatch that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Tieger. So the language issues, in the opinion of the Chamber, was dealt with in that decision and others. So if you have something further, I would like you to put it in writing and file a motion before the Chamber. And as to the translation and remuneration and staff issues, that's for the Registry to deal with at the moment, and it is only when the fairness of the trial is affected that Chamber could intervene. That said, let us bring in the witness. While the witness is brought in, there's one further procedural matter, so when we go into or out of -- come out of the private session, we need to put some pause while -- because there is some lag in the French or other interpretation, in particular, French. So at the last session, some confidential information was broadcast when we -- while we were coming out of the private session. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I appreciate that. I neglected to mention explicitly one thing, and perhaps because it's so obvious, and that is that there are any number of witnesses whose testimony encompasses a number of components of the case, and of course they will appear, for example, in the early component, talking about all phases of what they observed, learned, and experienced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But it is not the case of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This -- this witness, he's not one of those witnesses that I'm alluding to in that comment particularly, but as the Court has seen, this witness's evidence does embrace not only 1995 but other aspects of -- of the events as well. But what I was referring to more are the -- our witnesses who come to testify about one component but -- in the context of one component but have significant evidence about other components as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, make yourself comfortable. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I'd just like to say that with a trial of this magnitude, we need a system. We had Sanski Most. We had Pale, part of Sarajevo, now we have Zvornik and Srebrenica, and really, the absence of a system is felt, or chronology. It makes it more difficult. The already difficult position of the Defence in terms of resources and time. That's what I wanted to say for now. But secondly, I'd like to say that I'm a little worried with the efforts made by the Prosecutor to ensure protective measures for witnesses who are not victims. This witness is not a victim. This witness was a fighter for the BH Army, and I'm not allowed to mention the name of his village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, who is not a victim? Do you know my case at all, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking to the Trial Chamber now. I apologise. The two of us will discuss matters in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's totally unacceptable that you challenge the protective measures which was recognised by this court decision. There's other matters. You can appeal such decisions, but saying such words in front of the witness is not a proper way of challenging. Please continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I was thinking more about what Mr. Tieger intimated as to the future, and it just so happened that I mentioned this. But I don't want to insult anybody, of course, least of all the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I put it to you that the organisation, paramilitary organisation, secret organisation of the Muslims in Zvornik started in early 1991 with the creation of a whole network of units, both at municipal level and at regional level, for a number of neighbouring municipalities. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Well, what I have to say is this: What you're saying is a notorious untruth. First of all, we didn't have anything to organise ourselves with. We didn't have Slobodan Milosevic behind us to send in corps with tanks. And I remember very well, Mr. Karadzic, when I arrived from Belgrade to Karakaj, tanks were lined up. I don't know how many there were, 5, 10, 15, or how many, and all the barrels were trained on Zvornik. Now, if we had those, that kind of weaponry, then I would acknowledge that was so, but it was certainly not the way you just put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I put to you, Witness, that the detachment in your village was called the 6th Detachment -- now, I can't say the name of the commander. I can't utter the commander's name. Anyway, that he was a hodza, that is to say, an Islamic clergyman. Do you want to say that it wasn't that way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It wasn't. He wasn't a hodza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I put it to you and tell you that you had weapons, not hunting weapons but automatic weapons which was purchased in different ways, in an organised manner, and brought in to the entire municipality and to your village as well, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ064
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we had a few weapons, but they -- two soldiers arrested two of our men, and they handed over the little weapons that they had, whether they had procured it legally or not. Then those same soldiers turned up and asked us to surrender our weapons, and we did that too. Let me tell you who we surrendered them to. He didn't put his first and last name but just his last name was Cecaric. He was a warrant officer, Cecaric, and his first name began with an A, and you can find the man. Whether he was Aleksandar or Andrija, but anyway, it was A. Cecaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
